UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
BEFORE THE
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.
) Docket No.ER26-3650-000
JOINT COMMENTS,
REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION,
AND
LIMITED PROTEST OF THE LARGE ENERGY USERS
Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's ("Commission" or "FERC")
August 31, 2026 Combined Notice of Filings #1 and Rule 211 of the Commission's Rules of
Practice and Procedure,' the Coalition of MISO Transmission Customers iCMTC), the Illinois
Industrial Energy Consumers ("IIEC), the Association of Businesses Advocating Tariff Equity
("ABATE®), the NIPSCO Large Customer Group ("NLCG), the Louisiana Energy Users Group
("LEUG"), and the Texas Industrial Energy Consumers ("TIEC") (collectively, "the Large Energy
Users') submit these Joint Comments, Request for Clarification, and Limited Protest, to the
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. ("MISO) filing proposing revisions to its Open
Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff ("Tariff"), to establish certain
Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large Loads (the "IRR Proposal"). The Large Energy
Users appreciate MISO's work and responsiveness during the stakeholder process, but submit these
Comments and Limited Protest to ensure that the proposed Tariff language is consistent with the
underlying interconnection reliability objectives and to ensure that matters that significantly affect
rates are appropriately delineated in the Tariff and not reserved for future development in business
practice manuals.
1 18 CFR § 385.211.

RELEVANT BACKGROUND
On August 28, 2026, MISO submitted a Federal Power Action Section 205 rate filing
proposing revisions to its Tariff in response to the Commission's Order Instituting Proceeding
Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act? On August 31, 2026, the Commission issued
Combined Notice of Filings #1, which set the deadline for interested parties to file Comments by
September 18, 2026. CMTC, MLEC, and ABATE filed motions to intervene in the above-
captioned matter on August 31, 2026, September 2, 2026, and September 15, 2026, respectively.
TEC and the Louisiana Energy Users Group both filed a motion to intervene in the above-captioned
matter on September 14, 2026. TIEC filed a doc-less intervention on September 17, 2026. NLCG
plans to file a doc-less intervention on September 18, 2026.
The Large Energy Users are a collection of ad hoc associations of large industrial and
institutional end-users of electricity that consume substantial amounts of electricity at various
facilities throughout the MISO footprint. Members operate one or more manufacturing or large,
energy-intensive facilities in the MISO region and purchase electric delivery service or bundled
electric service from at least one MISO transmission owner. The Large Energy Users will be
directly affected by the outcome of this proceeding and have been active stakeholders contributing
to the Large Load Working Group, which informed MISO's development of the Tariff proposals.
The Large Energy Users greatly appreciate MISO's efforts to incorporate multiple
stakeholder perspectives into the proposed Tariff revisions. Stakeholder feedback has significantly
influenced the revised Tariff language and supports overall system reliability. While great strides
have been made towards consensus, under significant time and resource constraints, the Large
2 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal
Power Act, 195 FERC 1 61,212 (2026) (#Show Cause Order).
2

Energy Users file these brief Comments requesting clarification, and file a Limited Protest
requesting revised Tariff language.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The Large Energy Users appreciate the collaboration resulting from the Large Load
Working Group and MISO's willingness to listen to stakeholder concerns. These Comments focus
on two topics where the Large Energy Users submit that clarifications are necessary to ensure just
and reasonable practices affecting rates and to avoid adverse economic consequences and
unnecessary regulatory burdens to large loads, especially existing manufacturing and institutional
loads that have not triggered the regulatory and legislative efforts responding to concerns associated
with high-impact, large computational loads. First, the proposed tariff language in Section 37A
II.2(a) lacks an explicit exemption for existing loads in service that experience incremental growth
of less than 25 MW in total. Second, the proposed tariff language in Section 37A.4 is ambiguous
and, if not clarified, creates the possibility of burdensome real-time forecasting requirements for all
Large Loads including conforming or non-computational loads' where the terms of such real-time
forecasting requirements are not specified in the tariff, contrary to the Commission's Rule of
Reason requiring that practices that significantly affect rates must be clearly delineated in the legally
binding tariff on file with the Commission and not left to implement through non-binding guidance
at MISO's discretion (i.e., business practice manuals). The Large Energy Users emphasize that,
because current reliability efforts undertaken by the North American Electric Reliability
Corporation ("NERC") and federal legislation in the Ratepayer Protection Act focus on addressing
3 Similar to SPP's approved Tariff definitions and different reliability forecast requirements between Conforming
Load that is reasonably predictable and Non-Conforming Load that does not follow a predictable pattern, MISO's
proposed Tariff changes are to be applied differently depending on whether the Large Load consists of
Computational Load or instead is a traditional non-computational load, where the former is less predictable and
presents a greater risk to reliability that the National Electric Reliability Corporation is creating standards to address.
4 See https://www.nerc.com/standards/reliability-standards-under-development/2026-02-computational-loads (last
accessed Sep. 17, 2026).
3

large computational loads, the Commission must avoid approving unnecessary new regulations
and requirements for traditional manufacturing loads and non-computational loads.
II. _ COMMENTS AND LIMITED PROTEST®
A. The Commission Should Require MISO to Clarify Exemption Scenarios in
Section 37A I1.2 - Fully Exempt Large Load.
MISO's proposed Tariff language includes transition provisions which exempt certain
Large Loads. Section 37A II.2, subsection (a) states, "A Large Load that has a Service
Commencement Date on or prior to December 4, 2026, shall be exempt from all requirements set
forth in this Section 37A with respect to the portion of the Large Load that has procured
Transmission Service as of the Service Commencement Date. Any modification or series of
modifications to a Load that meets the MTEP/EPR Condition, which results in a cumulative
increase of 25 MW or more in Transmission Service for such Load and with a Service
Commencement Date after December 4, 2026, shall be subject to subsection (2)(b) belowi
Consistent with the feedback and MISO tariff drafts during the discussion of this issue
through the Large Load Working Group, it was represented by MISO and understood by the Large
Energy Users that existing loads in service were to be exempt from the new requirements until an
existing load grew by 25 MW or more, at which point the incremental amount of the Large Load
would be subject to the applicable requirements provided the resulting total load of the customer
is 50 MW or more. Based on the proposed Tariff language, the Large Energy Users request that
either MISO agree to clarify the proposed Tariff language or that FERC direct MISO to clarify the
5 See Exhibit A (federal legislation proposing a new federal standard for large loads that require electric energy
Ạprimarily to operate information technology infrastructure and related systems pertaining to data storage and
computational applications and servicesẠi).
• The Large Energy Users are generally supportive of MISO's filing, but have discrete substantive concerns, thus
necessitating requests for clarification and a Limited Protest, especially given our request for revised tariff language.
7 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.'s Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large Loads, Tab
A, Docket No. ER26-3650-000 (August 28, 2026).
4

proposed Tariff language to ensure that growth from existing loads is exempt from the new
proposed requirements, regardless of the timing of the increase, until such growth reaches 25 MW
by specifically including the exemption condition of increases less than 25 MW. To accomplish
this objective, the Large Energy Users propose the following additional redlined language:
(2) A Transmission Customer taking Transmission Service on behalf of a Large Load shall
ensure that all Large Load shall be subject to all the requirements as set forth in this
Section 37A, provided that:
Fully Exempt Large Load:
A Large Load that has a Service Commencement Date on or prior to
December 4, 2026, shall be exempt from all requirements set forth in this
Section 37A with respect to the portion of the Large Load that has procured
Transmission Service as of the Service Commencement Date, and shall also
be exempt from these requirements for modifications that result in a
cumulative increase in the Load of less than 25 MW after December 4,
2026. Any modification or series of modifications to a Load that meets the
MTEP/EPR Condition, which results in a cumulative increase of 25 MW or
more in Transmission Service for such Load and with a Service
Commencement Date after December 4, 2026, shall be subject to subsection
(2)(b) below. Any modification or series of modifications to a Load that
does not meet the MTEP/EPR Condition, which results in a cumulative
increase of 25 MW or more in Transmission Service for such Load and with
a Service Commencement Date after December 4, 2026, shall be subject to
subsection (2)(c) below.
If the above Tariff language is clarified, we respectfully submit that those proposed Tariff
provisions would then be just and reasonable. Accordingly, the Large Energy Users ask FERC to
direct MISO to clarify this language. Such directed clarification could occur through the issuance
of a deficiency notice rather than outright rejection of the entire filing without prejudice.
B.
The Commission Must Not Impose Unreasonably Onerous Real Time
Forecasts in Section 37A.4 for Non-Computational Loads
& "FERC may accept or reject the proposal. But as this Court has held, Section 205 does not authorize FERC to impose
a new rate scheme of its own making without the consent of the utility or Regional Transmission Organization that
made the original proposal." NRG Power Mktg., LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108, 114 (D.C. Cir. 2017). However, FERC
may issue a deficiency notice signaling that a Section 205 filing may be acceptable if certain deficiencies, such as
tariff language issues, are addressed and cured. See Midcontinent Indep. Sys., 196 FERC 1 61,134 at PP. 56-58, 104-
106 (2026).
5

1. A five-minute real-time forecasting requirement, as applied to non-
computational Large Loads, is unnecessary to ensure system reliability and
has not been demonstrated to be just and reasonable given such a
requirement would inflict unjustified significant burdens? and costs on end
users and manufacturers.
Section 37A.4 of the Proposed Tariff includes Large Load Forecast Data Requirements as
follows, "Prior to the later of the Service Commencement Date of a Large Load or September 1,
2027, a Transmission Customer taking Transmission Service on behalf of a Large Load must
provide day(s) ahead and real-time Load Forecasts for a Large Load directly to the Transmission
Provider to support the Reliability Assessment Commitment (RAC) and Security Constrained
Economic Dispatch (SCED) processes, along with other reliability studies. The Load Forecasts
shall be updated to reflect the most current information on the expected Demand, in accordance
with the Business Practices Manual for Large Loadại
This section appears to require a real-time forecast to support SCED, which implies a real-
time forecast updated every five minutes although this time interval requirement is not explicitly
stated in the proposed Tariff language. Requiring real-time five-minute interval forecasts for a six-
hour basis, updated every five-minutes'", would impose a substantial continuous operational,
analytical, and costly burden for Large Loads to provide without clear evidence that it will improve
the risks of inaccuracies within MISO's Reliability Assessment Commitment, Look Ahead
° In defining a significant burden for the proposed real-time forecast, end users would need to acquire/assign staff
with technical expertise to a new function to compute and submit data to MISO, or to the MISO Transmission
Customer, every five minutes twenty-four hours a day on a going forward basis with unknown methods to
potentially automate this work at additional expense. End user staff would need to forecast their operations and
resultant load values for not just a single day but compute a breakdown of this into 12 five-minute intervals per hour
of granularity, for each and every future hour, and submit this electronically with updates of the forward 72 five-
This detail of this real-time forecast requirements has been proposed in Section 3.2.1 of MISO's Business
Practices Manual #25 at the 8/25/26 Large Load Working Group meeting, available via the link below.
https://cdn.misoenergy.org/20260827%20LLWG%20Item%2011%200perational%20Forecasting%20BPM-025-
r14%20Draft 20(LLWG-2026-4A)771225.pdf

Commitment, or real time Security Constrained Economic Dispatch processes when compared to
MISO's current method of forecasting existing non-computational loads for these processes.
The FERC Show Cause Order included a concern that the reliability of the transmission
system could be at risk without greater visibility of Large Load additions; however, the Show
Cause Order did not specify the real-time forecast requirement in the manner currently proposed
by MISO in the proposed Tariff languageại Such real-time forecasting for all load, especially
non-computational load, is significantly burdensome and unnecessary, and MISO has not met its
burden under Section 205 of the Federal Power Act to justify the need for this requirement. The
Large Energy Users submitted further Joint Comments regarding this concern in the context of the
Large Load Working Group, which is attached hereto as Exhibit B.
2. Specific details regarding the real-time forecasting requirement are
inappropriately delegated to the Business Practices Manual.
The proposed language of Section 37A.4 of the Tariff imprecisely requires the forecasts to
"be updated to reflect the most current information" but does not include enough clarity for
affected market participants (and ultimately affected end users) to understand the significance of
the requirements and fails to explicitly indicate that MISO intends to impose not just an hourly
real-time load forecast requirement on non-computational and computational Large Loads, but
also a five-minute interval real-time load forecast requirement. Instead, MISO has deferred
development of the specific requirements to the non-binding Business Practices Manual. Such a
deferral is inappropriate when a requirement has the ability to inflict significant burdens and costs
on a market participant (which are then imposed on the end-user).
" Show Cause Order at P 64 noted a concern that "MISO's Tariff does not require transmission customers to
provide MISO hourly forecasts, telemetry data, and other data to ensure sufficient visibility..ạồi Emphasis added on
hourly as the Commission concern did not require consideration of more granular five-minute forecasts nor the
consideration of benefits versus the costs of providing such.
7

In City of Cleveland v. FERC, 249 U.S. App. D.C. 162, 773 F.2d 1368 (D.C. Cir. 1985),
the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals held that utilities must file, "only those practices that affect rates
and service significantly, that are realistically susceptible of specification, and that are not so
generally understood in any contractual arrangement as to render recitation superfluous."12 This
doctrine, known as the Rule of Reason, requires utilities to file with FERC practices that
significantly affect rates and service, and are easily reduced to writing. While the Rule of Reason
recognizes that there is an infinitude of practices affecting rates and services, 13 and affords the
Commission ample discretion to apply the rule as it sees fit, this discretion is not unlimited. In
Keyspan-Ravenswood, LLC V. FERC, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals found that The New York
Independent System Operator's ("NYISO) method for translating installed capacity into unforced
capacity should have been filed with FERC because the translation methodology reduced the
internal reserve margin by nearly a third which significantly affected its compliance with reliability
rules set by the New York State Reliability Council. 4
As discussed herein, a five-minute interval real time forecasting requirement is a costly
and burdensome proposal that would substantially affect rates and services and specifically the
operational costs of manufacturers across the Midwest. Similarly to NYISO's conversion
methodology at issue in Keyspan-Ravenswood, LLC v. FERC, the real time forecasting specifics
proposed in MISO's Tariff should be filed with FERC. As such, the details regarding the real time
forecasting requirement should be detailed in the Tariff, not in the Business Practices Manual.
And when the details are filed with FERC, new forecasting requirements must be just and
reasonable practices affecting rates. Taken together with undue burden that would be imposed on
12 City of Cleveland v. FERC, 249 U.S. App. D.C. 162, 773 F.2d 1368, 1376 (D.C. Cir. 1985).
13 Id.
14 Keyspan-Ravenswood, LLC v. FERC, 474 F.3d 804 (2007).

non-computational Large Loads by a five-minute interval real-time load forecast requirement,
FERC should clarify that any approval of MISO's proposed real-time load forecast requirement in
this proceeding is limited to requiring an hourly load forecast. If MISO wishes to purse a five-
minute real-time load forecast requirement, it must do so in a separate new filing with the
Commission explicitly requesting such a requirement - it may not impose such an additional
requirement through its Business Practice Manuals alone.
TV. CONCLUSION
WHEREFORE, the Coalition of MISO Transmission Customers, the Illinois Industrial
Energy Consumers, Association of Businesses Advocating Tariff Equity, the NIPSCO Large
Customer Group, the Louisiana Energy Users Group, and the Texas Industrial Energy Consumers
respectfully request that the Commission consider these Comments and direct MISO to clarify the
proposed tariff language, or, in the alternative, issue a Deficiency Notice directing MISO to
provide clarification regarding the issues discussed above.
Respectfully submitted,

Comments of the
Association of Businesses Advocating Tariff Equity (ABATE*),

Regarding
LLWG: Large Load Operational Forecast Requirements (LLWG-2026-4A)
September 10, 2026
ABATE, IIEC, LEUG, TIEC, CMTC, and MLEC as representatives of the End-Use Customer Sector, and IBEC
and NLCG as representatives of organizations advocating for large end-users, appreciate this
opportunity to provide these comments to MISO.
During the June 29, 2026 and August 27, 2026 meetings of the Large Load Working Group ('LLWG'),
MISO proposed details of the requirements for the Large Load forecast submissions in hourly and five-
minute cadences and notice that it plans to monitor forecast accuracy including the potential for
penalties? Specifically, due to concerns that large load additions could add substantial volatile demand
that MISO's current weather and calendar driven forecasting cannot capture and that FERC raised within
its recent Show Cause order, MISO proposes to require the following of all Large Loads, regardless of
whether they are Non-Computational or Computational:
• A forecast of five-minute integrated demand for the next five-minute period and the proceeding
71 five-minute periods, updated every five-minutes; and
• A potential monitoring period to measure Large Load forecast to actual error rates with
tolerance bands that could be applied to different types of Large Loads, and the potential to
assign torecast-related penalty costs to the Large Load errors that create them.
While we understand and agree with the need to address the possibility of large load additions
introducing substantial volatile demand that MISO's weather and calendar driven forecasting cannot
currently capture, MISO has not demonstrated: (i) a reasonable need for the five-minute integrated
demand portion of its proposal for Non-Computational Loads, or (ii) a need to design penalty charges at
this time.

Regarding five-minute interval load forecasts, the following are important considerations:
• MISO has not provided any evidence showing the lack of individual load five-minute demand
forecasts for existing 50 MW and larger Non-Computational Loads has resulted in either
significant reliability or cost subsidy issues within MISO over the last decades which have
included a very large number of 50 MW and larger Non-Computational Loads.
• It is the possibility of additional, very large amounts of new Computational Load not operated at
a very high, steady load factor that can be quickly dispatched up or down based on market
conditions which introduces a potential significant challenge to MISO's current weather and
calendar driven forecasting, not Non-Computational Loads.
• Putting aside demand response participation, that has its own Tariff and Business Practice
Manual requirements, MISO currently settles all load in the real-time market on an hourly
integrated demand basis, and not on a five-minute integrated demand basis. As a result, there
are no market signals that would cause loads that can quickly change their demand, specifically,
Computational Loads, to make abrupt five-minute changes in their demand.
• Requiring five-minute forecasts for a six-hour basis, updated every five-minutes, would impose a
substantial continuous operational, analytical, and costly burden for Large Loads to provide
without clear evidence that it will improve the risks of inaccuracies within MISO's Reliability
Assessment Commitment, Look Ahead Commitment, or real time Security Constrained
Economic Dispatch processes.
Given the above we urge that hourly forecast data provided day-ahead for Non-Computational Loads,
when combined with the newly required real-time telemetry for Large Loads, is sufficient for not only
day-ahead needs but also for real-time needs, until proven otherwise with actual data-driven
experience. There is no FERC requirement for real-time five-minute forecasts from Large Loads nor has
there been a showing of MISO reliability problems given existing Non-Computational Loads that
necessitates a new burden for customers. The FERC only noted a concern that "MISO's Tariff does not
require transmission customers to provide MISO hourly forecasts, telemetry data, and other data to
ensure sufficient visibility...'
As for MISO's proposed creation of incentives/penalties for Large Load forecast errors:
• MISO has not provided any evidence showing that participant submitted load forecast errors
have been significant and have resulted in reliability or cost subsidy concerns over the last
decades which have included a very large number of 50 MW and larger Non-Computational
• For many Non-Computational Loads, due to the nature of their processes, it is not possible for
them to forecast demand within a narrow band of accuracy on an hourly integrated demand
basis, never mind a five-minute integrated demand. As such, applying penalties to them for
falling outside a narrow band accuracy would not be just and reasonable as any lack of accuracy
forecast would not be a behavioral issue but rather related to the nature of the processes
associated with these loads.
2

• Without evidence of actual significant forecast errors in aggregate, as individual errors could
balance each other out due to their diversity, causing significant dispatch cost impacts there is
no basis for a new allocation of existing commitment, reserve, congestion, and/or shortage
pricing to loads based on the theoretical concept of uninstructed deviation or failure to follow
dispatch instructions for load as MISO suggests within its August 27, 2026 presentation.
• If penalties were applied to a Transmission Customer for forecast deviations without a
mechanism to separate errors from updated forecast deviations, and without mechanisms to
allocate charges appropriately between the Transmission Customer(s), Load Balancing Areas,
and retail Large Loads, then the resulting charges have the propensity to become a zero sum
incentive if they end up blindly being assigned to all load within a Load Balancing Area.
Given this, if it were demonstrated forecast inaccuracy for Non-Computational Loads introduced
significant reliability or cost subsidy issues that need to be addressed, which MISO has not shown to be
the case, the appropriate action would be to first, monitor such deviations and study their reasons, and
then secondly explore potential changes to the cost allocation for ancillary services, not the immediate
application of penalties to these loads without a full examination of actual occurrences and conditions.
Collected data can be monitored for potential impacts and accuracy incentives or penalties considered
later, if needed, around tolerance bands that are within the Load's control and based on actual
experience. 5
For the foregoing reasons, MISO should limit the application of its proposed real-time five-minute
forecast requirement to Computational Loads.
Also for the above reasons, MISO should not pursue forecast deviation incentives or penalties at this
time. An actual data-driven and risk-informed framework applied proportionally to demonstrated
reliability needs, system conditions, and facility characteristics makes the most sense at this time.
Thank you for providing us with an opportunity to submit our comments. The End-Use Customer Sector
appreciates the continued constructive dialogue on this issue and looks forward to continuing to work
with MISO and other stakeholders to deliver on MISO's commitment to reliability and MISO's Value
Proposition.
If it would be of help, we would be glad to discuss the above comments further with MISO and other
stakeholders. If you have any questions regarding these comments, please do not hesitate to contact
